segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 1: Library Workshop Registration

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Hi, I’m Mia. I’m calling about the library workshop on Saturday. Is it still open for registration?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Yes, it is. I’m Ben, the workshop coordinator. We still have a few places available, so you can still join.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Great. Can you tell me what the workshop is about?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Of course. It’s called “Research Basics”. It’s designed for students who are new to academic research. The workshop is led by a librarian, and it covers how to find reliable sources and how to cite them. These are skills that many new students need when they start writing academic papers.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: That sounds useful. When exactly is it?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: It’s on Saturday, the 15th of March, from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. The room is on the second floor, Room 204. Please arrive a few minutes early so we can start on time.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: OK. And how much does it cost?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: It’s free for students, but you need to register in advance. There are only 20 places, and they are given on a first-come, first-served basis. That means the earlier you register, the better your chance of getting a place.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: I see. How do I register?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: You can register online through the library website, or you can come to the front desk. But online registration is preferred because it’s faster. If you register online, you will receive a confirmation email with all the details.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Alright. Is there anything I need to bring?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Yes, please bring your student ID card and a notebook. You don’t need to bring a laptop, as computers are provided in the room. The notebook is useful because you may want to write down the main points during the session.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Good. Who is the workshop for? Is it only for first-year students?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: No, it’s open to all students, but it’s especially useful for those who are new to research. Postgraduate students are also welcome. In fact, we often have a mix of students from different years and subjects.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: OK. And will we get a certificate?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Yes, a certificate of attendance is given at the end of the workshop. But you must attend the whole session to receive it. The certificate can be useful if you want to show that you have taken part in extra training.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: That’s fine. One more thing: is the workshop in English?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Yes, it’s in English. But the librarian speaks slowly and clearly, so it’s suitable for non-native speakers. You should be able to follow the main ideas without difficulty.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Great. I’ll register online then. Thanks for your help.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: You’re welcome. See you on Saturday.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 2: Library Orientation: Research Help and Study Spaces

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Hello everyone, and welcome to the Westbridge University Library. My name is Sarah, and I’m the head librarian. This short talk will tell you about the help we offer and how to use our study spaces. Please listen carefully, because some rules have changed this year, and I want to make sure everyone knows about them before the busy part of the term begins.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: First, let’s talk about research help. The library has a team of subject librarians who can help you find books and articles for your assignments. Each librarian specialises in particular subject areas, so you can choose the person who best matches your course. You can book a one-to-one session with a subject librarian online. These sessions last thirty minutes, and they are free for all students. However, you must book at least one day in advance. If you come without a booking, we may not be able to see you immediately, because the librarians are often busy with other students.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Second, I want to explain how to use the study rooms. We have twenty group study rooms on the second floor. These rooms are equipped with whiteboards and large screens. You can reserve a room for up to two hours per day. Reservations are made through the library website. Please note that rooms are released if you are more than fifteen minutes late. So, if you are delayed, call the front desk to keep your room.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Now, about borrowing books. Undergraduate students can borrow up to ten books at a time. The loan period is three weeks. You can renew books online twice, unless another student has reserved them. If a book is returned late, you will be charged a small fine. The fine is fifty pence per day, per book. We send reminder emails three days before the due date, so please check your university email regularly.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Finally, let me mention our quiet study area. The quiet study area is on the third floor. It is a silent zone, so mobile phones must be turned off. Food and drink are not allowed in this area, but you can use the café on the ground floor. The library is open from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. on weekdays, and from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. at weekends. During exam periods, we stay open until midnight.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: That’s all for now. If you have any questions, please ask at the front desk. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 3: Week 28 Listening: Academic Stage Re-test and Process Description

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Good morning, Mia and Leo. I hope you're both well. Today we’re reviewing your academic stage re-test, and I want to go over the details with you so that you know exactly what to expect. Mia, can you explain the process you followed for the group project?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Yes, of course. First, we were given a topic by the department. Then we divided the work among the group members. After that, each member wrote a section. Finally, we combined the sections and checked for errors.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Good. That sounds like a clear and sensible process. Leo, what was the most difficult part?

segments.speaker: LEO
segments.text: The data analysis, because the software was updated just before we started. We had to learn the new version quickly.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: I see. That can happen. And Mia, how did you handle the references?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: We used a reference manager, which saved a lot of time. The citations were formatted automatically.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Excellent. Now, about the re-test. It will be held next Friday. The test consists of two parts: a written report and an oral presentation. The written report, which should be about 1,500 words, must be submitted by Thursday noon. The oral presentation will be given in small groups.

segments.speaker: LEO
segments.text: Will the presentation be recorded?

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Yes, it will be recorded for assessment purposes. But don’t worry—the recording is only used by the tutors.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: What about the marking criteria?

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: The criteria are explained in the handbook. You should read them carefully. The report is marked for content, organization, and language. The presentation is marked for clarity and interaction.

segments.speaker: LEO
segments.text: Is there a chance to get feedback before the final submission?

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Yes. You can attend a feedback session on Wednesday. The session, which lasts 30 minutes, is optional but recommended.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: I have another question. Can we choose our own topic for the report?

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: No, the topics are assigned by the tutor. However, you can narrow the focus within your assigned topic.

segments.speaker: LEO
segments.text: OK. And when will the results be announced?

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: The results will be posted on the noticeboard two weeks after the presentation. They are also sent by email.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Thank you. That’s clear.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: You’re welcome. Remember, the deadline is strict. Late submissions will not be accepted unless there is a medical reason.

segments.speaker: LEO
segments.text: Understood. We’ll start early.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Good. If you have any problems, email me. I check my email every morning.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 4: The Process of Academic Peer Review: A Lecture on Revision and Reassessment

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to explain the process of academic peer review, which is often used in universities. This process is designed to improve the quality of research papers before they are published. It is a system that many academic journals rely on, and understanding it can help you when you read or write research papers yourselves. Peer review also gives readers confidence that published work has been checked by other specialists, and it protects the reputation of the journal.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: First, a researcher submits a paper to a journal. The paper is then sent to two or three experts in the same field. These experts are called reviewers. They are usually experienced researchers who know the subject well. They read the paper carefully and provide feedback. The feedback is usually given in a written report. The reviewers may suggest changes, such as adding more data or clarifying the method. They may also comment on the structure, the writing, or the references. Reviewers normally work without payment, as a service to their academic community.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: After the reviews are received, the editor decides whether the paper should be accepted, revised, or rejected. The editor is the person who manages the journal and makes the final decision. If the paper needs revision, the author is asked to make the changes and resubmit it. This revision stage is very important because it helps to ensure that the research is accurate and well-presented. Authors usually receive a deadline for their revisions and must explain how they have responded to each comment.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Once the revised paper is received, it may be sent back to the reviewers for a second round of comments. This is called a re-review. The re-review process can take several weeks or even months, because the reviewers are often busy with their own work. Finally, when the editor is satisfied, the paper is accepted for publication. The whole process, from submission to acceptance, can take six months to a year. It is a slow but necessary process.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Now, let me give you an example. Imagine a paper about climate change. The reviewers might point out that the data analysis is not clear. The author then revises the analysis and explains it more fully. The revised paper is then checked again. This cycle continues until the paper meets the journal's standards.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: In conclusion, peer review is a collaborative process that involves authors, reviewers, and editors. It is not perfect, but it helps to maintain the quality of academic publishing. Thank you for listening.
